headline: All six Daunne bus crash victims named, but casualty counts still clash
dek: Police named driver Suresh BC among the dead, and one victim's surname changed between police reports, from Khatri to Gurung.
body_markdown:
A passenger bus travelling from Nepalgunj to Kathmandu crashed near Daunne in Nawalparasi East around 4am on Saturday, October 3, after its brakes failed, police told the Kathmandu Post. The bus went off the East-West Highway, Nepal's main Tarai road, and overturned into a roadside drain. Six people died.

By Saturday evening, police said they had identified all six, including the bus driver. The dead are Suresh BC, 36, the driver, of Khajura Rural Municipality-2 in Banke, and Dipendra KC, 32, of Kohalpur Municipality-3, Banke. Ekendra Raj Regmi, 55, of Kohalpur-10, Banke, also died. So did Krish Kanaujia, 22 (spelled Kanaujiya by Nepalnews), of Nepalgunj Sub-Metropolitan City-7, Banke. A 50 year old named as Nirjung Khatri by the Kathmandu Post, Peoples' Review and myRepublica, and as Nirjung Gurung in the final police account from Nepalnews and Radio Nepal, of Bheriganga Municipality-3 in Jajarkot, was also killed. Narendra Raj Giri, 65, of Swamikartik Rural Municipality in Bajura, was the sixth. Nepalnews and Radio Nepal reported the final list, both citing Deputy Superintendent of Police Anil Pandit at the Nawalparasi District Police Office.

For families on this route between the Tarai and the capital, a name on a police list lets grief, and the search for answers, begin. Thousands travel this route between Banke and Kathmandu every day, and families who send someone on it now have one fact they can hold onto.

## What the coverage missed

The basic count of who was on the bus still does not match. The Kathmandu Post and Ekantipur both reported 17 passengers, citing police. Nepalnews, myRepublica, Radio Nepal and Xinhua instead put the total at 18. Nepalnews's and myRepublica's earlier reports said that included the driver, with two people escaping unhurt. Seventeen passengers plus the driver would make 18. No outlet said whether the two figures count the same people.

The injury count moves just as much. Rising Nepal, Radio Nepal's first report, Nepalnews's first report, myRepublica and Xinhua all said 10 people were hurt. The Kathmandu Post and Nepalnews's identification update later said 12. Ekantipur said 11. Three different numbers, all sourced to the same police office, on the same day.

The identification itself came out in pieces. Peoples' Review first named only one victim, Nirjung Khatri. The Kathmandu Post and myRepublica then named five, with a sixth man, estimated at 40 to 42 years old, still unidentified. Hours later, Nepalnews and Radio Nepal said the sixth victim was the driver, Suresh BC, 36, younger than police had first guessed. That final police account, quoted directly from DSP Pandit, also changed the Jajarkot victim's surname from Khatri to Gurung, a mismatch that, as far as Nepal Wire could find, no outlet, including the two stories naming all six victims, flagged or explained.

None of that reached the cause. The Kathmandu Post, Xinhua and Ekantipur all reported, citing police, that the bus's brakes failed before the crash. The identification updates from Rising Nepal and Nepalnews do not mention brake failure at all.

## What we still do not know

Which passenger and injury figures are correct, and why police gave different outlets different numbers on the same day. The Nawalparasi District Police Office and DSP Anil Pandit could answer this.

Whether the Jajarkot victim's surname is Khatri or Gurung. Only Nawalparasi police can confirm which record is accurate.

Whether the bus, registration Province 3-01-006 Kha 1553, had passed a fitness inspection, and when that inspection last happened. The Department of Transport Management would hold that record.

Whether the government has announced compensation for the six families, including the driver's. No outlet has reported a compensation decision so far.

key_facts.fact: All six people killed in the Daunne bus crash, including driver Suresh BC, 36, have been identified by police.
Police told the Kathmandu Post the bus's brakes failed before it plunged into a roadside drain on the East-West Highway near Daunne.
The Kathmandu Post and Ekantipur reported 17 passengers were on the bus, while Nepalnews, myRepublica, Radio Nepal and Xinhua reported 18, including the driver, with two unhurt.

Reported injury counts ranged from 10 (Rising Nepal, Radio Nepal's first report, Nepalnews's first report, myRepublica, Xinhua) to 11 (Ekantipur) to 12 (Kathmandu Post, Nepalnews's update) on the same day.
Police named only one victim at first, Nirjung Khatri, before identifying five and then all six over the course of Saturday, October 3.
The final police account named the Jajarkot victim as Nirjung Gurung, while earlier reports from the same police office called him Nirjung Khatri.

social_hook: All six people killed when a Nepalgunj to Kathmandu bus crashed near Daunne have been named, but outlets citing police still give different counts of how many were hurt.
take: A Nepalgunj to Kathmandu bus crashed near Daunne, and it took police most of a day to agree on who died. Six names are now confirmed, including the driver, Suresh BC. But outlets citing the same police office reported three injured counts, two passenger totals and two surnames for one victim, all within hours. The Kathmandu Post, Xinhua and Ekantipur separately reported police blamed brake failure. Nawalparasi police owe these families, and every rider on this highway, one clean set of facts, not a different number every time.

caption.hook: Six people died on the Nepalgunj to Kathmandu bus near Daunne. Their families now have names. They still have no single count of how many were hurt.
caption.body: A bus bound for Kathmandu from Nepalgunj crashed near Daunne on the East-West Highway early Saturday, October 3. Its brakes failed before it overturned into a drain, police told the Kathmandu Post. All six dead are now named, including the driver, Suresh BC, 36. Yet outlets citing police reported different numbers all day. Some reports said 17 passengers, others 18 people including the driver. Injured figures ranged from 10 to 12. No inspection record or compensation decision has been made public yet. One victim's surname changed from Khatri to Gurung in the final police account. None of that has been explained.

angles.claim: The Oct 3-4 Daunne crash is at least the third brake-failure-linked bus crash on this same East-West Highway corridor through Nawalparasi district since 2023, yet none of the coverage, including the candidate stories, mentions this recurrence.
angles.why_it_matters: If the same stretch of highway keeps producing brake-failure crashes, the story is not an isolated tragedy but a road-safety and vehicle-fitness enforcement failure that affects every bus using this route, which matters directly to the thousands of Nepalis and diaspora travellers who use East-West Highway buses between the Tarai and Kathmandu.

evidence.fact: Police said the bus plunged into a roadside drain near Daunne after its brakes failed early Saturday.
A bus overturned at Dumkibas in East Nawalparasi on the East-West Highway in August 2023 after a brake failure, injuring 29.
Police estimated a brake failure caused a March 2025 crash on a bus travelling from Arghakhanchi to Bardaghat, in the same Nawalparasi corridor, killing four.
Police spokesperson Anil Pandit said a preliminary investigation indicated brake failure may have caused the October 2026 Daunne crash.

angles.claim: Same-day official and outlet figures for how many people were on the bus and how many were injured do not reconcile: some reports give 17 passengers and 12 injured, others give 18 people including the driver with 10 injured and two unhurt, and no later report explains the gap.
angles.why_it_matters: Families, insurers and investigators rely on an accurate head count; an unreconciled discrepancy of this size, in official police-sourced reporting on the same day, is itself a transparency problem the 'victims identified' follow-up stories did not flag, let alone resolve.

evidence.fact: The bus had 17 passengers on board and 12 others were injured, per police.
The bus carried 18 passengers from Nepalgunj; DSP Anil Pandit said 12 passengers sustained injuries.
There were 18 people including the driver on board; police said six died, 10 were injured and two escaped unhurt.
Radio Nepal's same-morning report said six died and 10 others were injured, with identities of the deceased not yet established.

angles.claim: Both stories chosen for this piece (Rising Nepal and Nepalnews) report only that victims were identified, omitting the brake-failure cause that competitor Kathmandu Post attributed to police on the same day, and omitting any quote from police, the hospital, or district officials about vehicle condition.
angles.why_it_matters: Running an identification-only story without the cause the police themselves gave to another outlet leaves Nepal Wire readers less informed than readers of the fuller same-day account, and risks the story looking stripped of the one fact, brake failure, that raises an accountability question.

evidence.fact: The Rising Nepal's identification update names DSP Anil Pandit but gives no cause for the crash.
Police told the Post the bus's brakes failed, causing the driver to lose control before it plunged into a drain.

angles.claim: Police released the names of the dead in at least three different stages within the same day, first one name, then five, then all six, including the driver as one of the deceased, without any outlet explaining why the count changed or how later names were confirmed.
angles.why_it_matters: A staggered, uncorrected identification count matters to families waiting for news and raises a basic process question, how Nepal Police verifies and releases victim identities in mass-casualty road accidents, that none of the same-day coverage, including the two candidate stories, addressed.

evidence.fact: Only one of six victims, Nirjung Khatri, had been identified as of the paper's first report, with the other five not yet established.
Five of the six victims had been identified, with police saying the sixth, an unidentified man, was yet to be established.
Police later identified all six individuals killed, including bus driver Suresh BC, as the sixth and final name.

investigation.summary: Nepal Wire can report what the identification-only follow-ups miss: police-sourced brake-failure crashes have now struck this same East-West Highway corridor through Nawalparasi at least three times since 2023, and the casualty counts given to different outlets on the same day, 10 versus 12 injured and 17 versus 18 people aboard, were never reconciled by anyone.

ranking.reason: Marginal and a day old, but well corroborated by at least eight outlets and not yet covered by us. It can be written responsibly only if the cause, failed brakes on an S-turn, is attributed to police via Kathmandu Post and the injured count dispute of 10 versus 12 is reported openly. Weakest dimension is comment friction.

Confirmed as a careful catch up piece. The crash happened on Saturday, October 3, at least eight outlets corroborate it, and we have not run it. Attribute the brake failure on an S-turn to police via Kathmandu Post. Report the 10 versus 12 injured and 17 versus 18 passenger gaps openly. Driver Suresh BC is among the dead, so nothing may imply fault beyond the police account. Weakest dimension is comment friction.

findings.passage: a 50 year old from Bheriganga Municipality-3 in Jajarkot; and Narendra Raj Giri
findings.problem: The article claims all six victims are named ('All six Daunne bus crash victims named'), and the body explicitly discusses a surname dispute over this same person (Khatri vs Gurung) later in the piece, yet the main list of the deceased never actually gives this person's name. A reader has no idea who this victim is, undercutting both the headline's core claim and the completeness standard (zero knowledge test). Kathmandu Post, Peoples' Review and myRepublica named him Nirjung Khatri; Nepalnews's final update and Radio Nepal's final update named him Nirjung Gurung.
findings.suggested_fix: Name the victim in the main list, e.g. 'Nirjung Khatri, or Nirjung Gurung in the final police account, 50, of Bheriganga Municipality-3 in Jajarkot' so the headline's claim that all six are named is actually true in the body, and so the later discussion of the surname discrepancy makes sense to the reader.

findings.passage: Krish Kanaujia, 22, of Nepalgunj Sub-Metropolitan City-7, Banke
findings.problem: The two outlets the article jointly cites for the victim list spell this name differently: Radio Nepal's final update spells it 'Krish Kanaujia' while Nepalnews's final update spells it 'Krish Kanaujiya'. The article silently picks one spelling and attributes it to both outlets without flagging the mismatch, even though the piece catches and highlights a similar name discrepancy (Khatri/Gurung) for another victim. This is an inconsistent editorial standard and a factual claim ('Nepalnews and Radio Nepal reported') that is not precisely true for the exact spelling used.
findings.suggested_fix: Either pick one outlet's spelling and attribute it only to that outlet, or note the spelling discrepancy the same way the Khatri/Gurung mismatch is noted.

findings.passage: The bus went off the Mahendra Highway, also called the East-West Highway, Nepal's main Tarai road
findings.problem: None of the listed sources refer to the road as the 'Mahendra Highway'; every source consulted (Kathmandu Post, Nepalnews, Radio Nepal, Peoples' Review, Xinhua, Ekantipur) calls it only the East-West Highway. Per house style, every claim must trace to a named source in the sources list, and this added name is not attributed to any of them.
findings.suggested_fix: Either drop the 'Mahendra Highway' reference or attribute it to a specific source if one uses that name; otherwise stick to 'East-West Highway' as the sources do.

findings.passage: For families on this route between the Tarai and the capital, a name on a police list is the fact that lets grief begin. That matters more than the crash site itself.
findings.problem: This is an editorial value judgment ('matters more than the crash site itself') not attributed to any source or fact in the record. House style allows taking a position the facts support, but this specific comparative claim is invented framing rather than a reported fact.
findings.suggested_fix: Rephrase to state the reader consequence plainly without an unsupported comparative judgment, e.g. 'For families on this route, a name on a police list lets grief, and the search for answers, begin.'

findings.passage: Nawalparasi police owe these families, and every rider on this highway, one clean set of facts, not five.
findings.problem: The 'take' asserts a specific count of five conflicting fact sets, but the body documents two passenger totals, three injury totals, three stages of naming and one surname swap, a jumble that does not cleanly add up to a verifiable count of five. The number reads as rhetorical rather than traceable to the body's arithmetic.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace 'not five' with a phrase that does not imply a precise, checkable count, e.g. 'not a different number every time.'

findings.passage: crashed near Daunne in Nawalparasi (Bardaghat-Susta East) around 4am
findings.problem: House style bans parentheses inside sentences ('No parentheses. Use a new sentence.'). This construction and a similar one later in the piece violate that binding rule, and parenthetical asides are harder to read on a quick scroll, hurting shareability.
findings.suggested_fix: Rewrite as two sentences: 'A passenger bus travelling from Nepalgunj to Kathmandu crashed near Daunne in Nawalparasi East around 4am on Saturday, October 3.'

findings.passage: Police named driver Suresh BC among the dead, yet outlets still disagree on how many were aboard and hurt.
findings.problem: The dek is supposed to add new information beyond the headline, but 'outlets still disagree on how many were aboard and hurt' largely restates the headline's own 'casualty counts still clash.' Only the driver's name is genuinely new information here.
findings.suggested_fix: Lead the dek with the driver fact and add a distinct new detail, e.g. the surname mismatch, rather than repeating the headline's clash framing.

findings.passage: Nepalnews and the Kathmandu Post then named five, with a sixth man, estimated at 40 to 42 years old, still unidentified.
findings.problem: The sources list's own description of the Nepalnews article used for this stage says it was 'used_for: naming five victims, 18 on board, 10 injured, two unhurt, named injured patients,' which describes naming injured patients rather than clearly confirming it named five deceased victims matching the Kathmandu Post's list. The underlying claim is probably right given Kathmandu Post content, but the Nepalnews half of the attribution is not clearly supported by the source metadata provided.
findings.suggested_fix: Verify the exact Nepalnews article text names the same five deceased as the Kathmandu Post before keeping the joint attribution, or attribute this detail to Kathmandu Post and myRepublica, which clearly state it.

findings.passage: The Mahendra Highway carries daily buses between Banke and Kathmandu, and every household that sends someone on that road waits for exactly this kind of confirmation when news of a crash breaks.
findings.problem: This reader consequence line is reasonable but slightly overreaches by implying a universal daily ritual of waiting for crash confirmations for every household on the route, a generalized emotional claim no source quantifies. It also repeats the unsupported 'Mahendra Highway' name flagged separately.
findings.suggested_fix: Tie the reader line more tightly to the record, e.g. 'Thousands travel this route between Banke and Kathmandu every day, and families who send someone on it now have one fact they can rely on.'

findings.passage: a mismatch no outlet, including the two stories naming all six victims, flagged or explained
findings.problem: This sentence implies a specific failure of diligence by named outlets (Nepalnews, Radio Nepal) without those outlets having had the chance to respond, and it is presented in Nepal Wire's own voice as a confirmed omission. It is likely accurate based on the sources reviewed, but asserting what competing outlets failed to do, in declarative voice, carries some risk if either outlet published a correction elsewhere that was not checked.
findings.suggested_fix: Soften slightly to 'a mismatch that, as far as Nepal Wire could find, no outlet has flagged or explained' to acknowledge the limits of the check.

red_team.summary: The reporting on casualty counts, injury totals and the staggered identification is well supported by the cited outlets, and the brake failure omission claim checks out against the actual Nepalnews and Rising Nepal text. The piece's biggest flaw is internal: it promises all six victims are named yet never actually gives the Jajarkot victim's name in its own list, undercutting the headline and confusing readers exactly where the story's investigative value is highest. Smaller issues include an unsourced 'Mahendra Highway' label, an uncaught spelling discrepancy in a victim's name that the piece should have caught given it flags a nearly identical surname dispute, and a couple of house style violations (parentheses, a dek that mostly repeats the headline). None of the problems found rise to defamation risk, since all contested claims are properly attributed to named outlets and police, and the piece is relevant and shareable as a road safety accountability story for Tarai to Kathmandu bus travelers.

responses.response: The red team is right. The piece spends a paragraph debating whether this victim is a Khatri or a Gurung but never puts either name in the main list, so the headline's claim that all six are named is not actually delivered in the body. That is a real completeness failure.

responses.proposed_edit: A passenger bus travelling from Nepalgunj to Kathmandu crashed near Daunne in Nawalparasi East around 4am on Saturday, October 3, after its brakes failed, police told the Kathmandu Post.

defense.summary: All ten findings hold up and are accepted with small, targeted edits. The most serious is f1: the article claims all six victims are named while actually leaving one person unnamed in the main list, directly undercutting both the headline and the zero knowledge test. f2, f3 and f8 are attribution precision problems, matching the piece's own stated standard for flagging name discrepancies and sourcing added facts. f4, f5 and f9 are unsupported editorializing or false precision that should be trimmed to what the record actually shows. f6 is a straightforward house style punctuation fix. f7 is a dek that under delivers new information. f10 needed a small hedge to avoid asserting a negative about competitors' full coverage. None of the findings required contesting; they are all cheap, specific fixes that make the piece match its own documented rigor.

rulings.note: High severity. The headline promises all six named, but the body list leaves the Jajarkot victim nameless. The defence edit fixes the name. The list must also drop its semicolons, which house style bans.
The piece must apply one standard to both name mismatches. The defence edit uses parentheses, which house style bans, so a rewrite is ordered below.
Mahendra Highway is the road's real formal name, but no listed source uses it. Dropping it costs nothing.
The comparative ranking is unsourced. The defence wording is acceptable.
'Not five' is false precision the body cannot cash.
Parentheses are banned. Only one instance exists in the body. The defence edit is fine.
The dek repeats the headline. The defence dek adds the surname change and fits under 160 characters.
The source metadata does not show that the early Nepalnews piece named the five dead. Narrow the attribution to the Kathmandu Post and myRepublica.
Sustained, but the defence fix brings in a new unsourced number, 'Thousands travel this route every day'. That edit is rejected. Use the sourced wording ordered below.
A modest qualifier on a negative claim about competitors is prudent. The defence edit is acceptable.
